sections.title: Overview
points: Cassandra is a distributed wide-column database. It partitions and replicates data to support large workloads and high write availability.
Design tables around known queries. Arbitrary joins and flexible cross-partition transactions are not its main strengths.

sections.title: Data Model and Primary Key
points: The partition key determines which replica set stores a group of rows.
Clustering columns order rows within that partition. They support bounded range queries in the required order.
A composite partition key hashes its combined values. Clustering columns do not independently distribute rows between partitions.
Limit partition size and traffic. Combining an entity ID with a time bucket can prevent indefinite partition growth.

sections.title: Partitioning and Replication
points: Consistent hashing assigns token ranges to nodes. Virtual nodes spread a physical node's ownership across multiple ranges.
Replication places copies on separate nodes. A topology-aware strategy also accounts for racks and data centers.
Any contacted node can act as the coordinator. It forwards the request to the replicas that own the partition.
Adding nodes changes ownership and requires data transfer. Rebalancing consumes capacity before the new distribution is ready.

sections.title: Consistency and Routing
points: Each operation selects a consistency level. This determines how many replica responses it needs to succeed.
Requiring more responses increases read/write overlap. It can also increase latency and reduce availability during failures.
Overlapping quorums do not make arbitrary concurrent, multi-record operations serializable transactions.
Lightweight transactions support conditional coordination for supported operations. Their additional coordination costs more than ordinary writes.

flows.title: Route a request through a coordinator
steps: The client sends a query and consistency level to a Cassandra node. That node becomes the coordinator for the request.
The coordinator hashes the partition key and identifies its replica set.
It sends the required read or write requests to those replicas.
The coordinator waits for enough responses to satisfy the selected consistency level. It returns a result or reports failure.

sections.title: Storage Model
points: A replica appends a mutation to its commit log. It then updates the in-memory memtable.
Flushing a memtable creates an immutable SSTable. Reads can combine data from memtables and several SSTables.
Bloom filters identify files that might contain a key. Indexes help locate the relevant data within those files.
Compaction merges SSTables and removes obsolete versions when safe. It consumes background CPU and storage I/O.
Deletes create tombstones. Keep them long enough to prevent stale replicas from restoring deleted values.

flows.title: Store a mutation and flush it to disk
steps: A mutation reaches a replica node.
The node appends the mutation to its commit log under the configured durability policy.
The node updates its in-memory memtable.
Later, Cassandra flushes the memtable into an immutable SSTable when a size or time condition triggers a flush.
After the relevant data is safely flushed, Cassandra can reclaim the corresponding commit-log data.
Background compaction later merges SSTables. The original write does not wait for a complete compaction.

sections.title: Gossip and Fault Tolerance
points: Gossip spreads membership and failure information between nodes.
Hinted handoff temporarily records writes for unavailable replicas. Repair or rebuilding is still necessary after longer gaps.
Choose replication and consistency settings for the expected failures. Acknowledging one write does not mean every replica has received it.

flows.title: Recover a missed write with hinted handoff
steps: A coordinator receives a write for a replica set.
One target replica is unavailable. The coordinator stores a temporary hint for the missed mutation when policy permits.
Available replicas process the write. The chosen consistency level still determines whether the client request can succeed.
When the unavailable replica returns, the coordinator sends the retained hint to it.
The replica applies the missed mutation. Longer outages can require repair because hints have limited retention.

sections.title: Data Modeling
points: Start with the required partition and range queries. Create tables that answer those queries directly.
Duplicate data into query-specific tables where needed. Define how updates keep those copies consistent.
For chat messages, partition by conversation and time bucket. Use an ordered message identifier as the clustering key.
Limit active conversation partitions. Retrieve recent messages from the relevant buckets instead of scanning unrelated conversations.

flows.title: Retrieve a page of conversation messages
steps: The application derives the conversation and time-bucket partition from the requested page.
It queries a limited range of message identifiers in the required clustering order.
Cassandra reads the relevant memtable and SSTable data for that partition.
The application returns the messages and a continuation boundary. It moves to an older bucket when needed.

sections.title: Examples and Advanced Features
points: For ticket browsing, partition detailed seats by event and section. This matches the view that opens one venue section.
A separate event_sections table stores section summaries by event. Browsing can tolerate lag; checkout must verify actual seat availability.
TTL can expire time-limited records. Expiry and frequent deletion create tombstones that affect read and compaction work.
Secondary indexes and materialized views support additional access patterns. They do not remove the need to control partition size and traffic.

sections.title: When to Use and Limitations
points: Cassandra fits large, predictable workloads with many writes and partition-local reads. Select consistency settings for each access path.
Complex joins, ad hoc relational queries, and cross-partition invariants can fit another database better.
Explain partition limits, replication, consistency levels, and repair. These choices determine how Cassandra supports the application.
